implementation_notes: Swift's `static let` (and a global `let`) is lazily initialised on first access, exactly once, even when several threads reach it simultaneously: the language guide states the guarantee for stored type properties, and the runtime implements it with swift_once, whose fast path is the same inline check as dispatch_once. The compiler therefore fuses laziness and thread-safe publication into an ordinary declaration, so the classic double check is never written. `lazy var` on an instance is the opposite case: the guide warns that simultaneous first access may initialise it more than once, so a shared per-instance lazy value needs explicit synchronisation (a lock, an actor, or an atomic state) - which is where the hand-written guarded form is still justified.
pitfalls: `lazy var` has no once-guarantee: two threads touching it first can both run the initialiser, so shared lazy state must live in a static let, an actor, or behind an explicit lock.
A stored property initialiser cannot throw, so a static let whose build can fail must return an Optional or trap - there is no way to propagate the failure to the first caller.
Accessing a static let while its own initialiser is running (directly or through a cycle between two types) deadlocks, because swift_once waits for the in-progress initialisation instead of failing.
The once check is paid on every access: for a value that is used in a hot loop, an eagerly built let (or an injected instance) is measurably cheaper.
